target_buyer: Electric utilities, energy infrastructure planners, engineering firms, municipal energy offices, project developers, and large-load/data-center planners
supporting_evidence: FERC reported that rapidly growing large loads such as data centers are driving new transmission and energy-supply needs and that these loads often seek the fastest available grid connection.
DOE's 2026 draft National Transmission Needs Study identifies pressing transmission needs driven by load growth from data centers, manufacturing, and other large industrial loads.

IEA's Electricity 2026 grid analysis identifies grid capacity as a critical bottleneck and reports record connection queues, with grid build timelines materially longer than many new data-center projects.

ERCOT reported approximately 410 GW of large-load interconnection requests after receiving 198 new requests in Q1 2026, demonstrating substantial study and planning workload pressure in at least one major U.S. region.

MISO describes an unprecedented surge in large-load interconnection requests from data centers, advanced manufacturing, AI computing facilities, and other energy-intensive industries, many seeking connection within 18-36 months.
CBRE's H1 2026 North America data-center research states that power availability and infrastructure delivery timelines remain decisive site-selection factors.

JLL's 2026 global data-center outlook reports multi-year grid connection waits in primary markets and describes operators pursuing self-generation, PPAs, private wire, and storage to work around grid constraints.
counter_evidence: FERC warns that speculative and duplicative large-load interconnection requests can clog queues, distort forecasts, and overstate realized load growth; queue size therefore cannot be treated as equivalent to real buyer demand.
CBRE identifies land, permitting, zoning, community opposition, fiber, and local approvals alongside power availability, so grid availability is not the sole site-selection constraint.

JLL notes that self-generation, private-wire arrangements, PPAs, and storage can mitigate grid-delay pain for some projects, reducing the value of a workflow that only reports grid constraints without evaluating alternatives.
risks: Engineering and infrastructure decisions can be safety-critical and must remain under qualified human review.
Public grid, interconnection, zoning, and permitting data can be stale, incomplete, jurisdiction-specific, or non-comparable.
Large-load queues can contain speculative or duplicative requests and must not be presented as realized demand.
The workflow must not claim licensed engineering analysis, utility approval, legal clearance, or authoritative site-selection decisions.
Third-party research and data must be used under applicable licensing and access terms; the product should store provenance rather than copy protected implementations.
next_action: Advance only to a bounded product specification focused on evidence collection, normalization, option comparison, provenance, and human-review preparation. Separately validate buyer willingness to pay before commercial launch.
claim_boundary: This independent review supports the existence and recurrence of grid/interconnection/site-selection friction and the plausibility of a decision-support workflow. It does not prove product-market fit, customer willingness to pay, engineering correctness, legal compliance, or commercial readiness.
